extracted.intended_audience: general news readers interested in tech/social media moderation and free-speech debates
extracted.subtask_description: Describes how a social platform (Twitter) applied its content-moderation policies to a satirical outlet (The Babylon Bee), including what counted as a violation and the consequences for repeat infractions. Covers perspectives from a former safety chief, a civil-rights instructor, and the platform owner on policy scope and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforce policies consistently ('same rules for everyone')
rubrics_metrics.description: "You can like the policies or you can dislike the policies, but it’s the same rules for everyone," (Yoel Roth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roth emphasizes that written platform policies were applied uniformly; enforcement decisions are tied to the policy text in effect. The owner can change policies later, but at the time cited the written rule was enforced as written.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for repeated policy violations
rubrics_metrics.description: "When you repeatedly tweet violations of a policy there are consequences, including account timeouts, and ultimately they can lead to suspension."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement follows a progression: warnings/timeouts for violations can escalate to suspension if violations are repeated. This progression was cited as the basis for the Babylon Bee action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misgendering as a violation of Twitter's hateful conduct policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The satire outlet lost its account for violating the platform’s rules on "misgendering," defined in the article as identifying someone with pronouns other than those they prefer, or that don’t align with their chosen gender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article frames misgendering as falling under Twitter's hateful conduct policy; content that misgenders public figures can be treated as disallowed conduct under that policy leading to enforcement actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting and victimization of vulnerable groups as a basis for removal
rubrics_metrics.description: Targeting and the victimization of the trans community on Twitter is described as "very real, very life-threatening, and extraordinarily serious," with examples of "orchestrated campaigns" singling out a vulnerable group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material that participates in or enables coordinated targeting of already-vulnerable groups (e.g., trans people), even when framed as satire, is treated as dangerous and can justify content removal or account suspension because it contributes to an unsafe environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform moderation constrained by owner's interpretation of free speech vs. law
rubrics_metrics.description: Elon Musk's stated position: when he touts "free speech" for Twitter, he only means "that which matches the law," and he is "against censorship that goes far beyond the law."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This view implies a narrower set of platform content restrictions (limited to legal bounds) and signals that policy scope and enforcement can change depending on owner/operator stance; removing platform-level protections (e.g., hateful conduct rules) would limit moderation options and could increase harm to vulnerable users.
